title: Shared Research Projects
keyIdea: Research means finding out facts to answer a question. A shared research project starts with a research question that facts can answer, like 'What do hedgehogs eat?'. We gather information from sources: non-fiction books, experts, and things we have seen ourselves, but not made-up stories. We keep only the facts that answer the question, jot them down as notes in a few key words, and put them together as a group, once each, with no opinions.

kid: Research means finding out. We start with a question, like: what do hedgehogs eat? A good research question has facts for an answer.

Next we look in sources. A source is where facts come from. A fact book is a source. So is an expert, like a park ranger. What you saw yourself counts too. A story book is made up, so it is not a source of facts.
A book has lots of facts. We only keep the ones that answer our question. 'Hedgehogs eat beetles' helps. 'Hedgehogs have spines' is true, but it is not about food.
Then we write notes: just a few key words, like beetles, worms, slugs. Last, we put all our facts together on one class poster, each fact once.
adult: This is the early research strand of writing. US Common Core asks children from kindergarten to Grade 2 to participate in shared research and writing projects (W.K.7 to W.2.7) and to recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question (W.K.8 to W.2.8). The English National Curriculum adds retrieving and recording information from non-fiction in Years 3 and 4. The vocabulary is research question, source, fact, non-fiction, notes and key words.

The skill is a cycle: ask a question, choose sources, pick out relevant facts, record them briefly, then share them as a group. Young children's own experience is a legitimate source ('Grandpa saw a hedgehog eat a slug'), and so is asking an adult who knows; what matters is that the information is real and answers the question.

Common mistakes: choosing a topic word ('Hedgehogs') or an opinion question ('Do you like hedgehogs?') instead of a question with a factual answer; treating a story book as a source of facts; collecting every interesting fact, even ones that do not answer the question; copying whole sentences as notes; and repeating the same fact or adding opinions ('the cutest') to the group's writing.

In the lab your child picks a research question, checks four sources with a magnifier, sorts facts that answer the question from true facts that do not, taps key words to make notes, and builds a class poster that leaves off a repeat and an opinion.

familyTip: Pick a question at bedtime, like 'How long do cats sleep?'. Next day, find out together from one non-fiction book or website and one person who knows. Write three key-word notes on a sticky note and share what you found at dinner.

visual.caption: Our question is 'Where do penguins live?'. Does each fact answer it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Penguins live near the South Pole.
Penguins live in the sea and on land.
Some penguins live on warm beaches.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: choose a research question, check sources with a magnifier, keep facts that answer it, tap key words for notes and build the class poster.

practice.prompt: Which one is a research question?
practice.hint: A research question asks something, and facts can answer it.
practice.explain: 'How do bees make honey?' has a fact for an answer. 'Bees' is only a topic, and 'Are bees nice?' asks for an opinion.

practice.prompt: Our class found {n} facts about frogs. Our question is 'What do frogs eat?'. Which fact do we keep?
practice.hint: Keep only the facts that answer our question about food.
practice.explain: Out of the {n} facts, we keep 'Frogs eat insects.' because it is about food. The others are true but answer other questions.

practice.prompt: Which is NOT a good source of facts about real lions?
choices: A story about a lion who talks
practice.hint: Which one is made up, and so not real facts?
practice.explain: A story is made up, so a talking lion is not a fact. A non-fiction book and a zoo keeper give real facts.

practice.prompt: {n} children all found 'owls hunt at night'. How many times does it go on our poster?
practice.hint: Does saying it again tell us anything new?
practice.explain: Once. It is one fact, even if {n} children found it. Repeating it adds nothing new.

choices: Finding out facts to answer a question
pool.hint: Research starts with a question you want to answer.
pool.explain: Research means finding out facts to answer a question.

pool.hint: Books and experts are both one of these.
pool.explain: A source is where facts come from: a non-fiction book, an expert, or something you saw.

pool.prompt: Good notes about 'Snails eat leaves and fruit in the garden' are…
choices: Snails eat leaves and fruit in the garden
pool.hint: Notes are a few key words, not the whole sentence.
pool.explain: 'leaves, fruit' are the key words. Copying the whole sentence is not notes, and small words are not key words.

pool.prompt: Dad saw {n} ducks on the pond. We are finding out where ducks live. Can we use what Dad saw?
choices: Yes, it is his own experience
pool.hint: Things people really saw can be a source too.
pool.explain: Yes. Dad really saw {n} ducks on a pond, so it is a fact from his own experience.

pool.prompt: Which one should NOT go on our class fact poster?
pool.hint: One of these is how someone feels.
pool.explain: 'The best pets' is an opinion. A fact poster has only facts.

pool.prompt: We found {n} facts. Which one answers 'How long do cats sleep?'
choices: Cats sleep for a lot of the day.
pool.hint: Look for the fact about sleep.
pool.explain: Only 'Cats sleep for a lot of the day.' is about sleep. The other facts are true but answer other questions.

pool.prompt: What do we do first in a shared research project?
pool.hint: You need to know what you are finding out.
pool.explain: First we ask a research question. Then we look in sources, make notes and share.
